para: The nature of dark matter is an open question at the heart of fundamental physics. Over the past century, independent observations have established that the visible matter we can detect — stars, gas, dust — accounts for only a small fraction of the total matter content of the Universe. Flat rotation curves in spiral galaxies [1, 2], the dynamics and gravitational lensing of galaxy clusters [3], and the detailed pattern of temperature anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) [4] all point consistently toward a dominant, non-luminous matter component. These observations, spanning scales from individual galaxies to the observable Universe as a whole, converge on the ΛCDM model, in which approximately 85% of the matter density is composed of cold, non-baryonic dark matter [4]. The non-baryonic character of this component is independently confirmed by Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN), which constrains the baryon density to Ωbh2 ≈0.022 — far below the total matter density Ωmh2 ≈0.14 measured by the CMB [5].

para: The evidence discussed in the previous section suggests that dark matter constitutes the dominant form of matter in the Universe and that it cannot be made of Standard Model particles. This conclusion opens a large parameter space of possible candidates: viable masses span roughly ninety orders of magnitude, from ultra-light bosonic fields with m ∼10−22 eV that behave as classical waves on galactic scales [32] up to macroscopic primordial black holes. In this section, we narrow our focus to the candidate class which is most relevant to Chapters 4through 8 of this thesis: weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). In fact, the so-called WIMP miracle — the observation that a thermal relic with electroweak-scale mass and coupling naturally reproduces the observed dark matter abundance — has made WIMPs one of the most compelling paradigms over the past two decades.

para: WIMPs constitute one of the most popular cold dark matter candidates. They have masses in the GeV–TeV range and interact with Standard Model particles through weak-scale couplings. They are produced through thermal freeze-out in the early Universe, a mechanism we describe in detail in Section 1.2.2. The observation that a particle with weak-scale mass and coupling naturally yields the observed relic abundance — the WIMP miracle — has made WIMPs one of the dominant paradigms in the dark matter field for over two decades. para: Axions are among the most popular alternatives to WIMPs, and as direct-detection limits on WIMPs have tightened, they have drawn growing attention from the dark matter community. The axion was originally proposed by Peccei and Quinn [37] as the pseudo-Nambu–Goldstone boson of a spontaneously broken global symmetry introduced to solve the strong CP problem of QCD [38, 39]. It acquires a small mass at the QCD phase transition, and an initial misalignment between its field value and the potential minimum sources a coherent oscillating condensate that today behaves as cold dark matter. This misalignment mechanism [40–42] is generic to any light scalar with a late-developing potential and naturally explains why such a feebly coupled particle can saturate the observed relic density. Because axions are bosons, they evade the Tremaine–Gunn bound and can sit at occupation numbers N ≫1, behaving as a classical field rather than as a gas of quanta. The phenomenologically viable range of axion masses is broad, spanning roughly 10−12 to 107 eV once astrophysical, cosmological, and laboratory bounds are combined [43, 44].

para: Consider a hypothetical species χ in chemical equilibrium with the Standard Model plasma of the early Universe, sustained by pair-annihilation reactions χχ ↔SMSM that proceed in both directions at equal rates. As the Universe expands and cools, two processes run in competition: the cosmological expansion, which dilutes everything and lowers the temperature, and the annihilation rate, which depends on the density of χ particles still available to find each other. Eventually the expansion wins: the reactions become too slow to maintain equilibrium, the comoving number density stops tracking its equilibrium value, and whatever population remains is locked in as the relic abundance we observe today. para: A particle that annihilates strongly enough stays in chemical equilibrium for a long time: it follows the equilibrium population as the latter drops exponentially, and only departs from it when the equilibrium abundance has already become small. Such a particle leaves behind few relics. A particle that annihilates weakly, by contrast, loses contact with the bath earlier, while its equilibrium abundance is still relatively large, and therefore freezes out at a higher residual density. In the thermal-relic context, the weakest particle wins. The dark-matter abundance is set by how little a candidate annihilates, not by how massive it is. The velocity-averaged annihilation rate 〈σvrel〉sets the relic abundance to first approximation, while the mass enters the final answer only logarithmically, through the temperature at which decoupling occurs.

para: Sommerfeld enhancement. A second class of corrections arises when dark matter couples to a mediator with mass MV ≪Mχ. The long-range attractive force distorts the incoming-pair wave function and enhances the annihilation probability at low velocities, a non-perturbative effect known as the Sommerfeld enhancement [69, 70]. The enhancement factor S scales as S ∝1/vrel in the Coulomb regime vrel ≪παg, saturates at vrel ∼MV/Mχ for Yukawa mediators, and can exhibit resonant peaks at specific mass ratios where a zero-energy bound state appears in the dark-sector potential. Halo velocities vrel ∼10−3 c therefore probe a regime in which S can reach O(102–103) [69], while freeze-out velocities vrel ∼0.2 c see only moderate enhancement. The Sommerfeld effect is essential for heavy electroweak WIMPs — the pure wino at Mχ ∼3TeV, the higgsino near Mχ ∼1.1TeV, and Minimal Dark Matter candidates more generally — where it shifts the thermal-relic mass from hundreds of GeV to multi-TeV scales. We return to this point in Section 1.4 when discussing J-factors and the loop-suppressed channels of Minimal Dark Matter. For the pure wino in particular, the enhanced halo rate at vrel ∼10−3 c is large enough that current gamma-ray constraints effectively rule the candidate out for cuspy halo profiles. For the GeV-scale candidates relevant to the Galactic Center excess analyzed in Chapter 4, by contrast, the standard thermal cross section fits the observed signal without invoking Sommerfeld enhancement, as Daylan et al. para: The classify-and-count approach, whether implemented with hand-crafted cuts or ML clas- sifiers, suffers from three interrelated problems that compromise the statistical rigor of the resulting constraints. First, no dark matter subhalo has ever been identified, so the “DM” class used in supervised classification has no empirical anchor and the resulting classification proba- bilities cannot be calibrated against reality. [AA: review this statement] Second, the posterior probability p(k|x) produced by any discriminative classifier absorbs the class prevalences of its training set (Section 3.4.2). When classifiers are trained on balanced datasets—with artificially equal fractions of AGNs, pulsars, and simulated DM sources—the resulting predictions reflect these imposed priors rather than the true composition of the gamma-ray sky. The same prior shift problem arises when a model trained on associated sources, where extragalactic objects dominate, is applied to the unassociated population, which has a substantially higher Galactic fraction. Correcting this bias requires a realistic testing set that mirrors the target population, but in the classify-and-count framework such a set cannot be constructed: the true class prevalences among unassociated sources are unknown, and for the DM class no confirmed example exists at all. para: The preceding chapters looked for localized dark matter signatures: the concentrated gamma-ray emission expected from the Galactic Center — where the dark matter density reaches its peak — and from individual subhalos that remain unresolved among the unassociated sources detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope. Neither strategy returned a definitive signal. The Galactic Center excess persists, but a decade of increasingly sophisticated analyses has not resolved the fundamental degeneracy between a dark matter annihilation origin and a population of unresolved millisecond pulsars [71, 193, 194, 209]. The search for dark matter subhalos among unassociated sources [243] found no significant evidence for an anomalous population at current sensitivity levels, consistent with theoretical expectations — a result that establishes competitive constraints but does not close the door. We then moved to studying the unresolved gamma-ray sky. At the population level, the source-count distribution and probabilistic catalog constructed in Chapters 6 and 7 mapped the unresolved gamma-ray sky to fluxes roughly 50 times below the detection threshold [307, 309, 343], characterizing the astrophysical landscape in which any dark matter contribution must reside, but without working on isolating a signal.
